Furthermore, several sewage sites are connected to the Yamuna River, a critical tributary of the Ganges, which amplifies the potential environmental and public health implications due to downstream contamination risks.
Despite its significant industrial and environmental importance, Faridabad remains underrepresented in antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance, particularly in environmental studies. Additionally, the proximity of our research institute to Faridabad enabled systematic, precise, and routine longitudinal sampling, which is essential for robust temporal analysis and understanding of AMR dynamics in heterogeneous sewage systems.
We have incorporated this detailed justification into the revised manuscript (Lines 484–492) to provide readers with clear context on the sampling strategy and coverage.
Comment #4. A spatial map indicating the geographical spread of the sampling locations is essential for informing the readers about the study’s extent of coverage. Both of the above can be included in the supplementary information.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In response, we have developed a comprehensive spatial map illustrating the geographical distribution of all sampling locations across the different cities and states included in the study. This map provides a clear visual representation of the study’s spatial coverage, helping readers better understand the extent and
8
diversity of the sampling effort. The spatial map has been included as Supplementary Figure S7 in the revised manuscript.
Comment #5. Lines 522 & 523 – The authors mention pure antibiotic but fail to mention the manufacturer and the purity of the standards used for their instrumentation. Details must be provided for readers benefit and for reproducibility.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful query regarding the source and purity of the antibiotic standards used in our study. To ensure analytical rigor and reproducibility, we utilized high-purity standards for all 11 antibiotics analyzed. All standards were procured from Sigma Aldrich (St. Louis, USA) with purities ranging from 95.5% to 99.9%, depending on the compound. Specifically, ampicillin (99.9%), azithromycin (95.5%), nalidixic acid (99.8%), amoxicillin (99.9%), kanamycin (99.9%), erythromycin (99.9%), rifampicin (97.7%), tetracycline (99.9%), spectinomycin (99.9%), polymyxin-B (99.9%), and colistin (99.9%) were employed.
These details, including the manufacturer and exact purity for each antibiotic standard, have now been incorporated in the revised manuscript as Supplementary Table S1 to enhance transparency and facilitate reproducibility.
Comment #6. The figures pack too much information and as a result, the text has become unreadable. Revised higher quality images are requested from the authors with larger and legible fonts in the images for better readability.

Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable feedback regarding figure clarity and readability. We acknowledge that some of the original figures contained a large amount of information, which impacted the legibility of text and data presentation. In response, we have revised all figures to enhance image quality and increased font sizes to ensure clear and legible labelling.
To further improve readability, we have divided several complex figures into smaller, more focused panels. For example, the phylogeographical analysis figure has been split into two parts: the primary portion is now presented as Figure 8 in the main manuscript, while the
9
supplementary portion has been relocated to Supplementary Figure S4. Similarly, Figure 9 (a–c) has been divided, with panels (a–b) retained in the main text and panel (c) moved to Supplementary Figure S5.
We trust these revisions substantially improve the clarity and accessibility of the figures and meet the journal’s standards for presentation.
Reviewer #2
Comment #1. The manuscript titled “Antibiotic Contamination and AMR Dynamics in the Urban Sewage Microbiome: Insights from a Longitudinal surveillance” gives a comprehensive analysis of the presence of antibiotic residues, antimicrobial resistance genes and the resistant pathogens in urban sewage in six cities in India. Though the study uses a multi-pronged approach that includes mass spectrometry (QTRAP), dipstick-based molecular assay, 16S rRNA metagenomics, shotgun metagenomics, and bacterial isolate analysis to decipher the AMR scenario in six Indian cities, it fails to provide the direct statistical correlation/ comparison of these parallel approaches. A systematic comparative analysis of these approaches combined with statistics could have provided strong evidence of the selection pressures driving AMR in the wastewater and could have improved the impact of the study further.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful and constructive comment. We would like to clarify that our study indeed incorporates a systematic comparative analysis of the multiple approaches employed. Specifically, mass spectrometry was used to quantify antibiotic concentrations in sewage samples, providing a direct measure of environmental antibiotic contamination. In parallel, dipstick-based molecular assays enabled rapid detection of key antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs) in the same samples, offering a high-throughput overview of resistance potential. Furthermore, we utilized 16S rRNA and shotgun metagenomic sequencing to comprehensively assess microbial diversity and the functional capacity of the resistome. Complementing these, whole-genome sequencing of cultured bacterial isolates provided strain-level resolution and enabled precise identification of genetic contexts of resistance genes, including their co-localization with mobile elements. Crucially, we conducted statistical analysis across these complementary experiments including ARG abundance, and microbial community structure. As suggested by the reviewer, a correlation plot (Supplementary Fig. S2) has been incorporated in the revised
10
manuscript. These analyses offer strong evidence of the selective pressures driving AMR emergence and dissemination in urban wastewater ecosystems. Comment #2. MK Madhukar, N Singh, VR Iyer, DT Sowpati, KB Tallapaka, RK Mishra, SC Moharir, Antimicrobial resistance landscape in a metropolitan city context using open drain wastewater-based metagenomic analysis, Environmental Research Volume 252, Part 1, 1 July 2024, 118556, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envres.2024.118556
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable suggestion and have complied accordingly.

Comment #3. Figure numbers are not put on the Figures. This makes it confusing to review the figures.

Comment #4: The labelling in Figure 1 should match with the description in the respective figure legend (line no 707- 710). It is not clear how the significance is calculated- what is the control group with which comparison is made to calculate the p value using t test.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable observation. In response, the figure legend has been revised to ensure consistency with the labelling in Figure 1 and to provide a clearer
11
and more accurate description (Lines 938-946).

The differences in sample numbers were primarily due to logistical constraints and sample quality issues during processing. Nonetheless, we ensured that the selected samples were representative of each site and time point to maintain the integrity and comparability of the dataset.

sample origins and their corresponding initials are as follows:

However, we respectfully wish to retain the term “longitudinal” in a specific context within the manuscript (Line 188), where it accurately describes the study design and sampling strategy for Faridabad, Haryana. These time-series samples were used across multiple analyses, including mass spectrometry (QTRAP), dipstick-based molecular assays, 16S rRNA metagenomics, and shotgun metagenomics.
Comment #9: Are the same 100 samples used for QTRAP Mass Spectrometry, used for dipstick-based molecular analysis? If yes, then proper comparative analysis should be performed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important and insightful query. In response, we have carefully analyzed the datasets and confirm that 51 out of the total samples used for QTRAP mass spectrometry-based antibiotic detection were also tested using the dipstick-based molecular assay for ARG detection.
As per the reviewer’s suggestion, a proper comparative analysis was conducted using these 51
13
matched samples to evaluate the relationship between the detected antibiotic (QTRAP) and the presence of corresponding antimicrobial resistance genes (dipstick assay). The results of this analysis are now provided in Supplementary Table S3a.
Additionally, we have incorporated a detailed description of this comparative analysis in the Results section (Lines 128–133) and further contextualized its significance in the Discussion section (Lines 508–519) of the revised manuscript.
Furthermore, many of these same samples were also subjected to shotgun metagenomic and 16S rRNA sequencing. This integrative, multi-platform analysis supports our central conclusion that antibiotic contamination in wastewater acts as a key selective pressure driving the enrichment and dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in the sewage microbiome.
Comment #10: Line 131- 132: Mention the mean and standard deviation for number of reads. This will give a sense of the distribution of number of reads across the samples.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestion. In response, we have now included the mean and standard deviation of the read counts to provide a clearer understanding of the sequencing depth across samples. This information has been added to the main manuscript (Lines 137–139) to better reflect the distribution and consistency of the sequencing data.
Comment #11: Line 171- since sampling was done only once from June to December, all the seasons are not covered. Mentioning it ‘seasonal’ variations is not appropriate. Inference about seasonality should be removed throughout the manuscript.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important observation. While the study spanned a 7-month period from June to December 2023-encompassing a substantial portion of seasonal transitions in the region-we acknowledge that the sampling frequency does not allow for robust conclusions on seasonality.
In compliance with the reviewer’s suggestion, all references to “seasonal variation” have been removed from the manuscript. Instead, we now present the data as a month-wise comparison, which more accurately reflects the temporal resolution of the sampling. These revisions have
14
been incorporated in the Results section (Lines 200–210).
Comment #12: Line 172- The microbial diversity varied across different locations (line 133- 143). In that case, pooling the data from these 6 locations for each of the months to analyse the temporal patterns is not appropriate.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this important observation and fully agree that microbial diversity is expected to vary across geographically distinct locations. To clarify, the section titled “Temporal variations in sewage microbiome” focuses exclusively on samples collected longitudinally from Faridabad, Haryana over a seven-month period (June to December 2023). No data from other states were pooled for this temporal analysis. This approach allows us to assess within-city temporal dynamics without confounding spatial variability.
Furthermore, in the revised manuscript, we have expanded our analysis to compare microbial profiles across samples collected from six different states of India—Assam, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Uttarakhand, and Haryana (Faridabad)—at a common time point. This cross-sectional inter-site comparison highlights spatial diversity while maintaining temporal consistency. The results of this analysis are presented in Supplementary Figure S1e and discussed in the updated text to ensure clarity and appropriate interpretation (Lines 222-231).
We hope this resolves the reviewer’s concern.
Comment #13: Line 441- 442- comparative analysis of dipstick data and shotgun metagenomic data should be performed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable suggestion. In response, we have expanded our shotgun metagenomic sequencing dataset by including additional samples, bringing the total number to 167, as now reflected in the revised manuscript. Upon cross-referencing, we identified 75 samples that were common to both the dipstick-based ARG detection assay and shotgun metagenomic analysis.
A comparative analysis was performed on these overlapping samples to assess the concordance and complementarity between the two methodologies in detecting antimicrobial resistance genes (ARGs). The results of this analysis are presented in Supplementary Table S3b, and a summary of the findings has been included in the revised manuscript (Lines 251–254). This integrated comparison enhances the robustness of our conclusions regarding ARG prevalence and distribution, and underscores the value of using both rapid molecular screening and comprehensive sequencing-based approaches in AMR surveillance.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this inconsistency. To clarify, sewage samples were collected from six different states across India—namely Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Assam, West Bengal, Jharkhand, and the NCR region of Haryana (Faridabad). Within Faridabad, Haryana, samples were collected from seven distinct sites over a seven-month period (June to December 2023) as part of the longitudinal surveillance effort.
To avoid confusion, we have revised the manuscript to consistently refer to these pan-India collection sites as “states” rather than “cities” (see updated text at Lines 40, 106-107, and 159; Table S11). Additionally, to enhance clarity and spatial context, a geographical map illustrating the distribution of sampling locations across the six states has been included in the revised manuscript as Supplementary Figure S7.
Comment #15: Line 507-510- more details on sampling needed. Were the samples collected in replicate for each sampling site for each time point? What was the sample collection method- grab sampling or composite sampling? What measures were taken to ensure that the sampling was unbiased and representative for that site for a particular timepoint? Was 30 ml sample enough to capture the complete picture? More details on sample processing before DNA extraction are needed. Was the sample processed/ concentrated? If yes, what method was used for sample concentration? What was the yield of the DNA? References are needed to support the methodology.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful queries regarding the sampling methodology and sample processing. In response, we have elaborated the details of the sample collection, processing, and DNA extraction protocols in the revised Methods section (Lines 611–622) to ensure transparency and reproducibility. Specifically, wastewater samples were collected using the grab sampling method in sterile bottles during morning hours, consistent with established protocols in similar studies with some modifications (Hendriksen et al., 2019; Tucker et al., 2022). For the longitudinal study in Faridabad, Haryana, samples were collected biweekly (twice in a week) over seven months (June–December 2023) from seven distinct sites. The geographical coordinates and detailed descriptions of all sampling sites across the six states are provided in Supplementary Table S11.
These methodological details have been incorporated into the revised manuscript, supported by relevant literature references to validate our approach.
Comment #16: Since dipstick assay was standardized in this study only, a comparison with a gold standard assay like RT-PCR would be required to ensure that the assay is efficient and sensitive. Data to support the sensitivity and specificity of the dipstick assay should be provided. The advantage of the assay over RT-PCR and the pros and cons with respect to the sensitivity, specificity and ease of use should be discussed.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful and valuable comment. We fully agree that benchmarking the dipstick assay against a gold standard method such as RT-PCR is important for validating its sensitivity and specificity.
The dipstick assay employed in this study was adapted from protocols successfully utilized in our recent publications for detecting bacterial species and viral variants (Talukdar et al., 2024, iScience DOI: 10.1016/j.isci.2024.111238; Paul et al., 2025, Front. Microbiol. DOI: 10.3389/fmicb.2024.1459644), where the assay demonstrated robust performance.
Notably, in certain instances, the dipstick assay detected resistance genes that were not identified by shotgun sequencing, suggesting potentially higher sensitivity of the assay in these contexts. Conversely, a small number of ARGs identified by shotgun sequencing were not captured by the dipstick assay, likely due to sequence variability affecting probe hybridization efficiency.
We have expanded the discussion section (Lines 520-533) to explicitly address the comparative advantages and limitations of the dipstick assay relative to shotgun metagenomics, including considerations of turnaround time, cost-effectiveness, operational simplicity, and suitability for deployment in low-resource settings. While shotgun sequencing remains the comprehensive gold standard, the dipstick assay offers a rapid, scalable, and cost-efficient alternative for targeted ARG surveillance, particularly valuable for large-scale or resource-constrained environments.
These additions serve to contextualize the dipstick assay’s utility, sensitivity, and specificity within the broader framework of AMR monitoring technologies.
Comment #17: The study provides insights into the AMR scenario in the urban wastewater through a multi-prong approach. The utilization of chemical, molecular, microbiological and bioinformatic techniques provide a comprehensive picture of AMR scenario. However, the study could have utilized the shotgun metagenomics more effectively to identify the non-bacterial AMR contributors, correlated antibiotic concentrations with ARG abundance, and critically evaluated the methodology. Also a detailed and systematic analysis for at least one year could have provided insights about the seasonal and longitudinal patterns of AMR and pathogens in wastewater.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful feedback and recognize the importance of the points raised. Regarding the utilization of shotgun metagenomics to identify non-bacterial contributors to antimicrobial resistance (AMR), we would like to clarify that our study employed a well-established metagenomic DNA extraction protocol optimized primarily for bacterial cells (Bag et al., 2016; doi: 10.1038/srep26775). This method, while effective for
18
bacterial lysis, is less efficient in extracting DNA from organisms with more robust cell walls such as fungi and certain protozoa. Consistent with this, our shotgun sequencing data demonstrated that over 95% of reads were bacterial in origin, with minimal representation of non-bacterial taxa.
In response to the reviewer’s suggestion, we have expanded the shotgun sequencing dataset to include 167 samples, thereby enriching our analysis of bacterial-associated antimicrobial resistance genes. While this does not fully capture non-bacterial AMR contributors, it significantly strengthens the resolution of bacterial resistome dynamics across diverse urban sewage sites.
Regarding the temporal scope of our study, we acknowledge that a year-long longitudinal design would offer comprehensive insights into seasonal and temporal patterns of AMR and pathogen prevalence. However, we selected a seven-month period (June to December 2023) to balance technical feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and scientific rigor in establishing baseline data. Importantly, this timeframe encompasses major seasonal phases in Faridabad, including summer, pre-monsoon, monsoon, post-monsoon, autumn, and early winter, allowing us to capture key microbiome dynamics relevant to AMR dissemination.
We concur that future work extending over a full calendar year would be valuable to elucidate finer-scale seasonal trends and longitudinal shifts, and we have discussed this limitation (Lines 597-599) and prospect in the revised manuscript.

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the insightful queries regarding the sampling methodology and sample processing. In response, we have elaborated the details of the sample collection, processing, and DNA extraction protocols in the revised Methods section (Page Nos. 20-21; Lines 671–682) to ensure transparency and reproducibility. Specifically,
16
wastewater samples were collected using the grab sampling method in sterile bottles during morning hours, consistent with established protocols in similar studies with some modifications (Hendriksen et al., 2019; Tucker et al., 2022). For the longitudinal study in Faridabad, Haryana, samples were collected biweekly (twice in a week) over seven months (June–December 2023) from seven distinct sites. The geographical coordinates and detailed descriptions of all sampling sites across the six states are provided in Supplementary Table S11.
At each time point, approximately 200 ml of untreated wastewater was collected and immediately transported on ice to the laboratory to minimize compositional changes. Upon arrival, the sample was thoroughly mixed, and a 30 ml aliquot was centrifuged at 8,000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4°C to pellet microbial biomass. The supernatant was subsequently filtered through a 0.22 µm Millex GV syringe filter (Merck, Darmstadt, Germany) and stored at −80°C for LC-MS/MS analysis to quantify antibiotic residues. The resulting pellet was resuspended in 1.5 ml of nuclease-free water, with 100 µl inoculated into Brain Heart Infusion (BHI) broth for culturomics under both aerobic and anaerobic conditions. The remaining 1 ml was used for metagenomic nucleic acid extraction, which supported downstream 16S rRNA gene sequencing, dipstick-based ARG detection, and shotgun metagenomic analyses. The DNA yield from the concentrated biomass obtained from 30 ml of sewage was consistently sufficient for all molecular assays and culturomics studies, providing a comprehensive representation of the microbial community and resistome. To ensure unbiased and representative sampling at each site and time point, a fixed sampling point was chosen and consistently sampling was done from this sampling point each time. Further, samples were collected during early morning hours within a defined time window and ensured that there are no atypical activities near the sampling site. Additionally, fresh sterile sample bottles were used at each sampling to ensure that there are no cross-contamination.
These methodological details have been incorporated into the revised manuscript, supported by relevant literature references to validate our approach.

Regarding the temporal scope of our study, we acknowledge that a year-long longitudinal design would offer comprehensive insights into seasonal and temporal patterns of AMR and pathogen prevalence. However, we selected a seven-month period (June to December 2023) to balance technical feasibility, cost-effectiveness, and scientific rigor in establishing baseline data. Importantly, this timeframe encompasses major seasonal phases in Faridabad, including summer, pre-monsoon, monsoon, post-monsoon, autumn, and early winter, allowing us to capture key microbiome dynamics relevant to AMR dissemination.

General comments
Paul et al. present valuable insights into antibiotic contamination and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dynamics in the urban sewage microbiome. This well-structured study highlights sewage as a significant reservoir of AMR, integrating data on antibiotic concentrations (11 antibiotics from 7 different classes), 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and ARG richness. Notably, the authors have developed a dipstick-based assay for ARG detection, adding a practical and innovative dimension to the study.
By employing both culture-based and sequencing approaches alongside antibiotic analysis, the study provides a comprehensive assessment of AMR in urban sewage. The data are thoroughly analyzed and effectively summarized in well-constructed figures, with ARG quantification and associations with taxa clearly depicted through network analysis.
Moreover, data from Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs) on this topic are limited, and this study significantly contributes to the understanding of Environmental AMR in these regions. This study aligns with the One Health Approach for AMR. The inclusion of such data would greatly enrich the ongoing global dialogue on AMR and its management in resource-constrained settings. In addition, this study reflects the emerging trend of wastewater-based AMR surveillance, which is gaining traction globally as a cost-effective and comprehensive method for monitoring AMR in urban environments. However, while the study is robust and methodologically sound, the Introduction and Discussion sections require significant improvement to better contextualize the findings and enhance their broader relevance. Strengthening these sections would further elevate the impact of this important work. Additionally, the dipstick-based assay should be validated to ensure its reliability. Given the emerging importance of wastewater-based epidemiology, it would be fitting to publish the dipstick-based assay as a standalone methods paper rather than including it as a section under methods in the current manuscript. Furthermore, the sample volume collected for analysis is not convincing, and additional clarification or justification is needed for the approach taken.
The manuscript may be accepted after major revision, with the suggested improvements addressed to enhance clarity and the overall impact of the study.
The specific notes below may provide further clarification, and I hope they are useful to the authors for the revision.

This detection assay is an extension of our previously validated dipstick platform. The core platform,
25
workflow, and the detection principles remain consistent with our previously published work, but we have tailored the targeted ARGs and their probe design.
As suggested, we have now cited the dipstick references in the Introduction section of the revised manuscript (Page Nos. 3-4; Lines 99-103; Reference Nos: 7 & 8). We have also updated the discussion section of the revised manuscript emphasizing the advantages and limitations of the dipstick assay including considerations of turnaround time, cost-effectiveness, operational simplicity, and suitability for deployment in low-resource settings (Page Nos. 17-18; Lines 557-574).
Comment 11. The Supplementary Table 2 is not immediately clear, and at first glance, it’s difficult to understand what is being presented. Including a few lines of explanation or a brief legend would help readers better interpret the scheme, especially for those who may wish to adapt this approach in their own work. Providing clarity in this section would enhance its utility and accessibility.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s valuable feedback. To improve the clarity and interpretability of Supplementary Table 2, we have now incorporated a detailed legend which will help the readers to understand the presented information more readily and clearly. The modified legend “Table S2: Detection of antibiotic resistant genes (ARGs) using dipstick-based assay; "1" indicates the presence of the resistance gene in the sample, "0" denotes the absence of the resistance gene in the sample” have been incorporated in the updated supplementary Table S2 in the revised manuscript.
Results:
Comment 12. A correlation plot between the observed antibiotic concentrations and ARGs/community composition could be considered to verify the relevance of the authors' conclusion regarding the need for tailored antibiotic use. Currently, no attempt was made to correlate the different datasets, and including such an analysis would strengthen the argument by demonstrating a direct relationship between antibiotic presence and resistance gene dynamics.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestion. In response, we have included a correlation analysis plot in the revised manuscript as Supplementary Fig. S4 to evaluate the relationship between the measured antibiotics through LC-MS/MS and the abundance of antimicrobial resistance genes identified. This analysis was performed using spearman
26
correlation which revealed positive correlation between the macrolide antibiotics and the abundance of mph and msr genes, nalidixic acid with qnr & oqxB genes, kanamycin and spectinomycin residues with aad genes, and amoxicillin residues and bla gene. The relevant details and interpretations have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Page No. 9; Lines 287-293).
We believe that this integrated analysis strengthens our conclusions regarding the role of environmental antibiotic exposure in shaping resistomes and supports the need for tailoring use and context specific antibiotic stewardship strategies.
Comment 13. Line 142 What kind of ordination was performed?
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s query. In response, we would like clarify that two types of ordination analyses viz. 3D Principal Coordinates Analysis (PCoA) and 3D Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS) were performed, both based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity. These methods were employed to robustly visualize and validate the differences in microbial community structure across the samples. We have incorporated the complete details in the Statistical analysis section of the methodology part in the revised manuscript (Page Nos. 25-26; Lines 831-840).

In response, we have performed a 3D PCoA to better capture the variation in microbial communities, and the updated results have been incorporated into the main text (Page No. 6; Lines 192-195, Fig 3f). To further strengthen the analysis and provide a more comprehensive comparison, we also conducted a 3D NMDS analysis based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, as recommended. The NMDS results and plots have been included in both the main text (Page No. 6; Lines 192-195) and the supplementary materials (Supplementary Fig. S2b).

27
sewage samples from both community and hospital outlets in Faridabad, Haryana. These were assessed using both 3D PCoA and 3D NMDS and the detail finding have been incorporated in the revised manuscript (3D PCoA; Page No. 5; Lines 166-168, Fig. 3b) and (3D NMDS; Page Nos. 5-6; Lines 168-175, Supplementary Fig. S2a).
Comment 15. Line 162 – What was the basis for subsetting the data? It would be helpful to clarify the criteria or rationale used for selecting the specific subsets of data, as this will provide readers with a better understanding of how the analysis was conducted and ensure the approach is reproducible.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this valuable feedback. We expanded our shotgun metagenomic sequencing dataset to 167 samples to achieve higher taxonomic resolution and a more comprehensive characterization of microbial functions related to antibiotic resistance and its dissemination. The rationale and relevant information have now been incorporated into the revised manuscript (Page Nos. 6-7; Lines 201-211). The representative subset of these 167 samples was strategically selected to maximize analytical efficiency, ensuring robust and meaningful insights. The selection ensured comprehensive coverage across geographic distribution and temporal heterogeneity of the samples as well as representative from different sewage source types (e.g., community, and hospital-influenced sites).
This strategy enabled us to account for spatial and temporal diversity in antibiotic occurrence, aligning with the study’s objective to assess contamination patterns across diverse urban contexts. By ensuring a robust and representative sample, we believe this approach provide meaningful insights, strengthens the study’s goal and enhances its reproducibility.
Comment 16. Figure 5: The PCoA plot provides a useful visualization of microbiome variations across months; however, the first two axes explain only 35% of the variance (21% and 14%), suggesting that key patterns may exist in higher dimensions. To strengthen the analysis, the authors should explore alternative methods like NMDS and assess higher-dimensional variance using a scree plot or 3D PCoA. These could enhance the robustness and clarity of the findings.
Response: We sincerely acknowledge the reviewer’s constructive comment. In accordance with the suggestion, we performed a 3D PCoA, and the updated results have been incorporated into the main manuscript (Page No. 7; Lines 214-216, Fig. 5a). To further enhance the robustness and dimensional clarity of our findings, we also carried out a 3D NMDS analysis. The NMDS results, along with their visual representations, are now included in the main text
28
(Page No. 7; Lines 222-223) and in the supplementary materials (Supplementary Fig. S2c).
Additionally, to better understand temporal shifts in microbial community structure, we conducted a longitudinal, month-wise analysis of the sewage microbiome in Faridabad, with a specific focus on contrasting community versus hospital sources. The observed compositional differences were evaluated using both 3D PCoA (Page No. 8; Lines 248-253; Supplementary Fig. S3d) and 3D NMDS (Page No. 8; Lines 253-255; Supplementary Fig. S2d), and these results have been incorporated into the revised manuscript accordingly.
Discussion:
In my opinion, the Discussion is not as intuitive as it could be. Given the significant effort put into sample collection, processing, and data the analysis, the discussion could be improved to explain the observed clustering and seasonal differences more clearly. A more detailed interpretation of these results would help readers better understand the underlying factors driving the patterns observed, providing a stronger connection between the findings and the broader implications of the study.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. In response, we have revised the discussion section to provide a more intuitive and detailed interpretation of the clustering patterns and temporal variations observed in our data (Page No. 18; Lines 575-590).
Furthermore, we have clarified the broader implications of our findings to strengthen the impact of the study which are as follows:
• We have incorporated detailed clarification of the sample spread and also the justification behind choosing the Faridabad, Haryana for longitudinal sampling site (Page No. 16; Lines 514-525).
• We have incorporated a detailed description of the comparative analysis of the antibiotic residues detected in the samples through LC-MS/MS and the ARGs identified by dipstick-based detection assay (Page No. 17; Lines 544-556).
• We have expanded the discussion section to explicitly address the comprehensive comparison of the dipstick-based assay for detection of ARGs with shotgun metagenomics, including considerations of turnaround time, cost-effectiveness, operational simplicity, and suitability for deployment in low-resource settings (Page Nos. 17-18; Lines 557-574).
• We have also included detailed insights regarding the use of multi-prong approach to understand the comprehensive picture of AMR scenario in sewage water (Page No. 19-20; Lines 637-645).

Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation of our revised manuscript and for recommending it for publication. We greatly appreciate the precious time and effort, the reviewer has taken to assess our work and strengthen it throughout the review process.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have satisfactorily addressed most of my queries.
Response: We are grateful to the reviewer for the positive feedback on our revised manuscript and for acknowledging that the majority of the queries have been satisfactorily addressed. In addition, we have carefully considered few remaining points points and incorporated the necessary clarifications in the updated re-revised manuscript.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The manuscript addresses a relevant topic with potential implications for environmental monitoring and public health. However, in its current form, it suffers from several critical shortcomings that prevent it from making a meaningful contribution to the literature.
The overall discussion is weak and largely descriptive, with minimal critical interpretation and very limited comparison with existing data from the same region or from India more broadly, which significantly undermines the contextual relevance of the findings.
Response: The author appreciates the reviewer’s comment regarding its potential implication for environmental and public health approach. As per the reviewer’s suggestion, the authors have substantially revised the discussion by critically interpreting the results in the context of occurrence of antibiotic residues in the environment and providing a more critical comparison with previous studies from India and globally (Page Nos. 17-18; Lines 564-590). Specifically, we now discuss the frequent detection of amoxicillin and azithromycin in agreement with prior Indian studies (e.g., Mutiyar and Mittal, 2014; Arun et al., 2022; Akhter et al., 2023;
Overall, we have revised the discussion to provide a more balanced and informative interpretation by comparing our findings with prior Indian and global studies.
The methodology for sample preparation in the antibiotic analysis does not appear to follow standard or validated protocols. No evidence is provided that the current approach was validated, nor are technical or biological replicates described, raising concerns about the robustness and reproducibility of the data. While the manuscript states that eleven antibiotics were analyzed, no information is given on the limits of detection (LOD) or limits of quantification (LOQ), which are critical for assessing the reliability of reported concentrations as the current approach is not a standard one. The discussion of antibiotic residues is largely general and descriptive, without sufficient integration of the study’s own data. For example, the authors do not provide specific values for critical antibiotic in the result or discussion that could support interpretation of environmental or clinical relevance. Explanations for absence or presence of certain antibiotics remain speculative and are not linked back to quantitative data. Similarly, the presentation of the dipstick-based assay is superficial and lacks critical evaluation. The reliability, sensitivity, and known limitations of dipstick methods are not discussed, which is essential for interpreting the validity of the findings.
Response: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestion and have addressed it accordingly. In our study, sewage water samples were centrifuged and the supernatant filtered through a 0.22 µm syringe filter was used for LC-MS/MS analysis to detect antibiotic residues. While liquid-liquid extraction or solid-phase extraction methods are frequently employed to concentrate antibiotic residues from environmental samples, we performed the direct injection approach to detect and analyse the neat water samples for the presence of antibiotics. This simplified method helped to maintain the integrity of the antibiotics in their original form anticipated to be present in the sewage water sample and also minimizes analyte loss associated with multi-step extraction methods. The details of the sample preparation have been provided
3
in the methodology section of the manuscript (Page No. 22-23; Lines 741-746).
In our study, technical replicates were included to demonstrate reproducibility of the data, and in addition biological replicates were also represented by longitudinal sewage samples collected independently from the same location at multiple times points. To validate the approach, specifically we have assessed method Linearity (correlation coefficient R² from calibration curve, with concentration range), Precursor ion (m/z) values, and limits of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ), and other details have been incorporated in the revised manuscript. As suggested, we agree that reporting the LOD and LOQ is critical for assessing the reliability of the reported antibiotic concentrations. In the revised manuscript, we have now included the LOD and LOQ values for all eleven antibiotics, which were determined based on the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N) of 3:1 and 10:1, respectively following established guidelines. Comprehensive details of the LOD and LOQ values have been incorporated in the revised manuscript (Page No. 5; Lines 139-146 and Supplementary Table 1(l).
In response to the reviewer’s comment, regarding the discussion section of antibiotic residue, the authors have addressed it explicitly by linking our explanations with the quantitative data obtained in the study (Page No. 17; Lines 541-557). Specifically, now we have highlighted the highest detection frequency of kanamycin in 66.6% of the samples followed by spectinomycin (50%) and amoxicillin (45.1%) with overall concentration ranging from 0.416-18.711 ng/mL, along with the antibiotics such as erythromycin, tetracycline, nalidixic acid, and rifampicin detected in lower frequency (<15%) in the samples. We have also discussed the absence of ampicillin and polymyxins in the samples, which could be due to the higher degradation and instability in environmental conditions. Additionally, we have strengthened the comparative aspect of antibiotic residues by linking our quantitative findings with previous Indian studies and the details have been incorporated in the revised manuscript (Page No. 17 - 18; Lines 564-581, 584-590).
As per the reviewer’s suggestion, we have also expanded the details of the dipstick assay standardization in the methodology section of the revised manuscript (Page No. 23; Lines 760-768). The authors have also revised the discussion elaborating the evaluation of the dipstick assay mainly reliability, sensitivity and its limitation. The detailed information has been incorporated in the discussion section of the revised manuscript (Page No. 18; Lines 604-622).
We believe these inclusions in the discussion and methodology section of the manuscript have substantially reduced speculative interpretation, and improve the interpretability of our findings.
Therefore, I recommend rejection at this stage, with encouragement to submit an improved and more thoroughly revised version.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the constructive and thoughtful evaluation of our manuscript. We fully acknowledge the concerns regarding the methodological rigor, depth of data interpretation, and contextualization with respect to Indian and global studies. In the revised version, we have substantially strengthened the methodological section by
i) Providing details of the performance characteristics of the LC-MS analysis to detect antibiotic residues including details of linearity, limit of detection (LOD) and limit of quantification (LOQ), coefficient correlation for each antibiotic (Page No. 22; Lines 741-746).
ii) Strengthening the workflow of the molecular based dipstick-assay (Page No. 23; Lines 760-769).
We understand that integrating our findings with existing literatures will highlight the novelty and significance. So, as suggested, we have enhanced the discussion by directly comparing our results with relevant Indian and Global studies, highlighting both consistencies and divergences. Furthermore, we have refined the contextual analysis throughout the manuscript to better emphasize the novelty and significance of our findings in the revised manuscript (Page No. 16-17). Also, to strengthen the comparative context of our findings with previous studies, we have incorporated additional references, and are cited as References 15, 17, 19, 28, 39, 47-48 in the revised manuscript.
